title: Alternate Focused Work With Real Breaks
subtitle: Work Hard, Rest Well
description: Use a protected focus block followed by a real break, then adjust the length to your task, energy, and schedule instead of treating 90/30 as a biological rule.

lifeOsSource.hack: Protect one block for focused work, then take a real break before the next demanding block. Use 90/30 only as one possible starting pattern and adjust it to your context.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Choose one important task, protect a focus block from avoidable interruptions, then step away for a real break. Adjust both periods to your workload and energy rather than forcing a fixed 90/30 schedule.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Was the focus block long enough to make progress, did the break actually feel like a break, and what duration would fit the next cycle better?

faq.question: Do I need to work for 90 minutes and rest for 30?
faq.answer: No. Those numbers are one possible structure, not a biological prescription. Shorter or longer periods may fit your task and day better.

faq.question: What counts as a real break?
faq.answer: A break should reduce the demand you were just placing on attention. Step away from the main task, change posture or environment, and avoid turning the break into another work queue.

faq.question: What if meetings interrupt the pattern?
faq.answer: Plan around the calendar you actually have. One protected focus block can still be useful. The pattern should adapt to the day rather than become another schedule you have to defend.

intro.html: Focused work is easier to sustain when it has a boundary and is followed by a genuine change of pace. A 90-minute focus block and a 30-minute break can be one experiment, but Brali does not treat those numbers as a universal human rhythm.

sections.title: 1. Choose one demanding task
sections.html: Give the focus block a clear target: draft the section, review the dataset, solve the design problem, or prepare the proposal. A vague block called work is harder to protect.

sections.title: 2. Choose a realistic focus block
sections.html: Pick a duration that gives the task room without making the schedule fragile. Ninety minutes may suit some deep work; a shorter block may suit a meeting-heavy day or lower energy.

sections.title: 3. Remove avoidable interruptions
sections.html: Close unrelated tabs, mute non-urgent notifications, and keep a small note for things you remember but do not need to act on now. The goal is fewer unnecessary switches, not isolation from genuine responsibilities.

sections.title: 4. Take a real break
sections.html: When the block ends, step away from the main task. Walk, stretch, eat, rest your eyes, or do something light that does not simply replace one work stream with another.

sections.title: 5. Leave a clear next step
sections.html: Before the break, write one sentence about where to resume. This makes it easier to return without keeping the whole task active in your head.

sections.title: 6. Adjust the cycle
sections.html: After a few rounds, notice when attention faded, whether the break restored you, and how the schedule interacted with real work. Change the durations rather than treating the original numbers as a test of discipline.

editorialCuration.reason: Replace an inherited 90/30 article containing unsupported ultradian claims, fabricated productivity observations, prescriptive hydration/caffeine advice and rigid timing rules with a flexible focus-and-recovery practice.
